model.name: 2026/0292(CNS)
model.title: VAT fraud: extension of the application period of the optional reverse charge mechanism and Quick Reaction Mechanism

summary.lead: Official summary (Legislative Observatory, Legislative proposal published):

blocks.text: The European Commission proposes a Council Directive to extend until 30 June 2030 two temporary value added tax (VAT) anti-fraud tools in Directive 2006/112/EC: the optional reverse charge mechanism and the Quick Reaction Mechanism. The proposal follows the special legislative procedure under Article 113 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union; Parliament is consulted.
Purpose and context

The proposal aims to maintain targeted tools against VAT fraud, particularly Missing Trader Intra-Community (MTIC) fraud, during the transition to the digital reporting requirements under the VAT in the Digital Age (ViDA) package. Member States are to apply national measures transposing the cross-border digital reporting requirements from 1 July 2030.

Under the normal VAT rule, the supplier is liable to pay VAT. The reverse charge mechanism instead allows the recipient, where it is a taxable person, to account for VAT. This prevents suppliers from collecting VAT from customers and disappearing without paying it to tax authorities.
Extension of the reverse charge mechanism

The proposal provides for extending the period during which Member States may optionally apply the reverse charge mechanism to specified domestic supplies of goods and services susceptible to fraud. The deadline in Article 199a of the VAT Directive would move from 31 December 2026 to 30 June 2030.

The mechanism may be used in predefined sensitive sectors, including trading in greenhouse gas emission allowances, mobile phones, integrated circuit devices, game consoles, tablets and laptops, gas and electricity supplied to taxable dealers, raw and semi-finished metals, gas and electricity certificates, cereals and industrial crops, and telecommunications services.

The Commission notes that all Member States except Malta use the mechanism for at least one eligible category. Greenhouse gas emission allowance trading is the most frequently covered category, used by 22 Member States. Twenty-four Member States consider the mechanism useful in combating fraud.
Extension of the Quick Reaction Mechanism

The proposal also provides for extending the Quick Reaction Mechanism (QRM) until 30 June 2030. The QRM enables a Member State, in cases of imperative urgency and sudden, massive VAT fraud, to introduce a temporary reverse charge measure for goods or services not covered by the predefined categories.

The mechanism is subject to a rapid Commission procedure. The Commission must, within one month, either issue a negative opinion or confirm in writing that it has no objection. The Member State may adopt the special measure upon receiving that confirmation. The QRM can therefore cover the period needed to obtain a standard derogation under the VAT Directive, which requires a Commission proposal and unanimous Council approval.
Although the QRM has not been used in practice, 18 Member States consider that it should be retained, either unchanged or with limited adjustments.
Link with digital VAT controls

The proposed extension is intended as a transitional measure until the ViDA digital reporting framework becomes applicable. From July 2030, cross-border business-to-business supplies of goods and services are expected to be subject to near-real-time digital reporting and mandatory structured electronic invoicing in a standard Union format.

The framework also envisages a centralised VAT Information Exchange System (VIES) hub for cross-border reporting and taxpayer identification, giving tax authorities access to transaction-based information, including bank details. Member States may introduce domestic electronic invoicing and reporting obligations from 2025, subject to later alignment with Union standards.
Legal basis and financial implications

The proposal is based on Article 113 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and would amend Directive 2006/112/EC. The Commission considers Union action necessary because the extension of these VAT Directive mechanisms cannot be achieved by Member States acting alone.

The proposed measures remain optional and temporary. The Commission considers them proportionate to the objective of combating fraud and states that they would have no adverse effect on the Union budget or VAT-based own resources.

The European Commission proposes a Council Directive that would keep two temporary tools against VAT fraud in place until 30 June 2030. The measure extends the optional reverse charge mechanism and the Quick Reaction Mechanism, both of which are aimed mainly at fraud where businesses charge VAT and then disappear without paying it to tax authorities. The proposal is meant to bridge the gap until new digital VAT reporting rules apply.

Under the normal VAT rule, the supplier pays the VAT. Under the reverse charge mechanism, the business receiving the goods or services accounts for the VAT instead, which stops suppliers from collecting VAT from customers and vanishing. The proposal moves the deadline for this optional tool from 31 December 2026 to 30 June 2030. Member States may use it for a set list of sectors that are prone to fraud, such as greenhouse gas emission allowance trading, mobile phones, computers and tablets, gas and electricity, certain metals, cereals and industrial crops, and telecommunications services. The Commission notes that every Member State except Malta uses the mechanism for at least one category, and that greenhouse gas emission allowance trading is the most common, used by 22 Member States.

The Quick Reaction Mechanism would also be extended to 30 June 2030. It allows a Member State facing sudden, large-scale VAT fraud to introduce a temporary reverse charge for goods or services outside the standard list. The Commission must respond within one month, either with a negative opinion or written confirmation that it has no objection, and the Member State can act once it receives that confirmation. Although no country has used this mechanism so far, 18 Member States want it kept, either as it is or with limited changes.

The extensions are a temporary bridge to the wider VAT in the Digital Age framework. From July 2030, cross-border business-to-business sales are expected to be reported almost in real time and to use standardised electronic invoices, supported by a central EU hub that gives tax authorities transaction information. The proposal rests on Article 113 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, and the Commission argues that Member States cannot achieve this alone. The measures stay optional and temporary, and the Commission states they would have no adverse effect on the EU budget or VAT-based own resources.
